evaluation_raw.prompt:
Compare the before and after garment images after one robot handling action. Evaluate the action stage by stage instead of collapsing it into one useful flag. Use only directly visible evidence from the labelled RGB/depth files and the rollout video contact sheets listed at the end. Do not use or search for any other files, including perception JSON, metrics JSON, NumPy arrays, heatmaps, overlays, or MP4 files. The before/after views are static. When chronological rollout contact sheets are supplied, use them to assess acquisition, transport, and laydown over time; otherwise mark those stages UNKNOWN when jaw motion or layer identity cannot actually be established. Never infer success only because the commanded action should have produced it. When a height ridge or sharp relief is present, distinguish two hypotheses: (a) a separable overlapping layer, which should form a visible tent or hanging patch while far garment landmarks remain on the table, versus (b) a rolled wrinkle or local curl, which may only become taller, narrower, or more tightly curled when pulled. Height or gradient alone does not support target_structure_acquired. If the hold frame shows no independent hanging material, or shows the ridge tightening without footprint extension, mark the target structure contradicted/unknown and treat the lateral pull as untested. When a compression probe is visible, compare the selected peak with the immediately adjacent cloth during closure: if the peak-to-neighbour height difference clearly decreases, but no independent hanging patch appears and distant landmarks stay put, classify the event as `COMPRESSIBLE_SINGLE_PEAK`/rolled wrinkle, lower graspability confidence, and do not credit target-layer acquisition. If far landmarks move with the gripper, classify it as whole-garment drag rather than successful ply isolation. Judge progress toward the exact user objective: Fold the shirt into the five ordered steps and a neat compact stack.. Treat that objective as authoritative. Do not declare progress merely because the garment became more open or spread unless that change directly advances the named task. Use the target-selection, target-structure, transport, and laydown fields to record whether the named target was actually manipulated and reached the requested state. Do not invent numeric measurements. For visible_area_delta, overlap_delta, and relief_delta, use INCREASED, DECREASED, UNCHANGED, or UNKNOWN unless an exact numeric measurement is explicitly supplied.

The keep/change decision is mandatory and causal. Put every parameter or strategy that the evidence supports under keep. Put only the earliest failing/unsupported choice and necessary downstream choices under change. Do not change a supported grasp anchor or grasp depth merely because transport failed. For example, when acquisition and target-layer motion are supported but transport is insufficient, keep grasp_anchor and grasp_depth, and change pull_direction and/or pull_distance. When acquisition fails, treat contact location, jaw alignment, pre-close entry path, closure geometry, and Z as competing causal hypotheses. Do not recommend another height-only retry merely because the cloth is thin unless the visible evidence specifically isolates height as the cause. After repeated empty closes with the same contact geometry, next_experiment.change must include at least one non-height contact dimension. Do not name a privileged solution in advance; infer the next hypothesis from the observed failures. The change list must be non-empty when another safe grounded experiment exists. Use an empty change list only when the garment is already as open as this setup can reasonably achieve, or continuing is unsafe, visually ungrounded, or blocked by a hard physical/infrastructure condition.

Approved procedural skill library for duplicate checking:
### Skill: collar-full-shake (v1)
Purpose: Use a validated shirt-collar grasp to lift, shake open, transport, and lay the garment down so the collar structure can reveal the garment.
Guidance:
Use only after the visual collar decision and grounded Camera A grasp are validated. Keep the collar grasp orientation fixed and perpendicular to the collar. Lift to a controller-reachable high pose, center at Y=0, perform the host-owned shake-open maneuver, then move toward a useful +X location before retreating toward -X while descending through several waypoints. Keep descent and retreat balanced rather than making either one dominate, release only near the table after the garment has had room to spread, and retract/home afterward. Use current measured geometry and controller IK; never copy fixed coordinates, release in mid-air, or replace the collar with a shoulder or sleeve.

### Skill: controller-ik-recovery (v1)
Purpose: Recover safely when controller IK rejects a garment manipulation path before physical execution.
Guidance:
When controller IK rejects a pose or interpolated segment, preserve the supported visual objective but shorten extreme reach, lift, or transport; keep every waypoint inside the workspace, include a controlled release, and rerun preflight and controller IK before execution.

### Skill: direct-shake (v1)
Purpose: Test whether a validated garment grasp can open the cloth by lifting and shaking it without running the collar-specific transport and laydown routine.
Guidance:
Use after any grounded fabric grasp when the immediate experiment is only a shake response test. Lift to a controller-reachable high pose, keep the held fabric clear of the table, center if useful, run the host-owned shake maneuver, observe whether the garment separates or reveals structure, then lower and release in a controlled way. Do not add a long +X retreat or pretend that a shake-only result proves collar identity; preserve workspace, grounding, preflight, and IK checks and never use fixed coordinates.

### Skill: flatten-garment (v1)
Purpose: Progressively open and flatten a garment by validating the grasped structure, establishing a useful hanging configuration, transporting in a verified opening direction, and laying down only while the scene shows measurable improvement.
Guidance:
Follow this staged workflow:
1. Acquire a validated garment structure: choose a visible, liftable anchor whose local RGB-D measurement, height, and depth consistency support a real garment grasp; do not proceed from an unsupported or table-only point.
2. Establish a hanging configuration if useful: lift to a validated safe height and confirm that the grasped fabric is supported and can hang without dragging or colliding. If the lift does not reveal a supported structure, stop and re-plan.
3. Transport toward a verified opening direction: infer the direction from the current garment geometry and before/after evidence, then use validated intermediate waypoints with stable orientation and workspace margin. The farthest safe X direction is allowed only when the scene verifies that it opens the garment; do not assume it is always correct.
4. Continue only while overlap decreases or coverage increases: after each meaningful transport segment, compare the garment footprint, visible area, layer overlap, and height relief. Stop, release, or re-plan when the move is not improving those measures; never continue a blind pull.
5. Lay down progressively: retreat while descending through validated intermediate heights, release quasi-statically on a clean surface, and avoid dropping, flinging, twisting, or dragging the loaded gripper. The skill supplies this decision sequence, never fixed coordinates or robot API calls.

### Skill: grounding-plan-recovery (v1)
Purpose: Recover from an invalid or inconsistent grounded garment proposal before motion.
Guidance:
When grounding validation rejects a selected point or its use in the plan, reinspect the current evidence, choose a newly grounded visible fabric point, keep the path inside the workspace, include a controlled release, and rerun preflight and IK before execution.

### Skill: hold-checkpoint-timeout-recovery (v1)
Purpose: Interpret and recover from a garment run whose post-grasp hold verification could not be classified in time and therefore forced a local release, and recognize when 15 consecutive acquisition failures across diverse anchor classes with adequate depth definitively disprove single-anchor separation for a configuration and require infrastructure escalation.
Guidance:
Keep the existing rules: a failed-closed or timed-out hold check makes the observation evidence about the grasp only, the unexecuted transport must never be recorded as wrong in direction or distance, and the validated approach clearance, deposit region and quasi-static release carry over to the retry. Add this definitive escalation threshold with infrastructure acknowledgment: when a configuration has produced 15 or more consecutive acquisition failures across at least 5 geometrically distinct anchor classes (peaks, boundary bands, low-relief structures, raised rims, corners, raised edges, claimed free boundary lips) where adequate engagement depth was achieved (closure commanded at or below measured surface height, including compression-probe-recommended depths for high-relief structures and manual calculation for low-relief structures) and every attempt confirms no independent hanging material with all far landmarks remaining seated and hold checkpoint returning FAILED_CLOSED or timeout, treat this as definitive evidence that the garment configuration does not provide separable single-anchor structure. At that threshold, escalate to a two-contact strategy where one contact immobilizes a region through weight, pinning, or clamping while the second contact attempts separation, or target a mechanically verified free edge where the gripper can wrap around a confirmed fabric boundary with visible interior passage or light between plies on both sides. The critical insight: when high-relief structures (17+mm raised edges), medium-relief ridges (10+mm), low-relief corners (sub-4mm and 7mm range), raised plateau tents, compressed peaks, and claimed free boundary lips with adequate depth and varied entry axes (vertical, oblique, side) all produce identical empty-jaws outcomes, the anchor class variety itself and the entry axis variety have both been exhausted. State the infrastructure limitation explicitly when available primitives cannot execute true two-contact opposition: acknowledge that continuing single-anchor attempts is unsafe and ungrounded, and that no further safe grounded experiment is possible within current primitive constraints rather than attempting a 16th single-anchor variant. Preserve validated approach clearance, deposit region, planned pull direction and quasi-static release across the strategy change, since unexecuted transport carries no evidence about those choices.

### Skill: laydown (v2)
Purpose: Convert a garment held from a useful lifting anchor into a more spread tabletop configuration, and recognise when a release has re-piled the garment onto itself instead of opening it.
Guidance:
Keep the quasi-static procedure: let the garment hang under gravity, retreat away from the hanging cloth while descending through intermediate heights, let the hanging face become the upward face, and release in a controlled way. Add two checks. First, before descending, require the retreat to carry the grasp point beyond the horizontal extent of the material still hanging below it, onto clear table, so the fabric unrolls onto bare surface rather than settling back over the area it came from; a retreat shorter than the hanging garment's own reach should be treated as not ready for release. Second, after release, compare footprints rather than only position: if the deposited outline sits inside the previous outline, if previously exposed features such as prints, collars or hems have become covered, and if new steep fold walls appear in depth, judge the laydown a regression caused by too short a retreat, and plan the next deposit farther out across clean table instead of repeating the same descent from the same anchor.

### Skill: molmo-annotation-retry (v1)
Purpose: Recover from an auxiliary Molmo annotation worker failure before motion.
Guidance:
When auxiliary Molmo annotation fails before execution, preserve the saved perception evidence, retry the annotation on a fresh iteration, and never treat a missing semantic anchor as garment-state evidence; keep workspace, release, preflight, and IK validation mandatory before any later motion.

### Skill: null-change-missed-grasp-recovery (v7)
Purpose: Recognise a near-null garment action, separate a clean miss from a contact-without-hold on a compressible pile, and additionally reject a closure whose resolved anchor or engaged height is inconsistent with the visually chosen structure.
Guidance:
Keep the existing null-change and contact-without-hold checks and the escalation rule. Add a pre-closure consistency gate. Before the jaws close, confirm that the anchor the controller actually resolved corresponds to the structure that was chosen in the images, and that the engaged height falls inside the measured relief of that structure rather than collapsing onto the table plane. If the resolved contact point sits far from the visually selected feature, or if the engaged height is indistinguishable from the surrounding tabletop, treat the planned bite as ungrounded and re-ground before descending instead of executing it. Likewise, a local surface measurement taken at a different location, outside the working region, or on bare table is not grounding for the anchor and must not be used to justify a closure. When the resulting observation is a complete null change with every far landmark seated, record it as evidence about the anchor and the engagement geometry only, leave the untested pull direction, pull distance, deposit region and release choices intact, and make the next attempt at a differently structured opening rather than repeating the same descent.

### Skill: planning-timeout-recovery (v1)
Purpose: Recover from a Claude planning timeout before any garment motion starts.
Guidance:
When planning times out before execution, retain the exact failure context, start a fresh planning attempt from saved perception, keep all waypoints inside the workspace, include a controlled release, and rerun preflight and IK before execution.

### Skill: preflight-contract-recovery (v1)
Purpose: Recover from a rejected action schema or unsafe action sequence before motion.
Guidance:
When static preflight rejects a plan, keep only the high-level garment objective, correct the reported action contract or sequence, keep all waypoints inside the workspace, include an explicit release, and rerun preflight and IK before execution.

### Skill: translation-only-reanchor (v22)
Purpose: Recognize when repeated congruent relocations disprove single-anchor peeling for a garment, and additionally retire the terminal end-cap of a rolled bundle as a ply anchor once a perpendicular carry only relocates the whole bundle.
Guidance:
Keep the existing stop rule, the free-boundary verification requirement, and the mandatory lift-phase abort. Add this appearance lesson: the rounded end of an elongated cloth roll, even when it presents solid measurable relief above the table and reads as an end-of-structure boundary with a visible tuck, is not evidence of a separable ply. A roll end is continuous with the body, so carrying it across the table perpendicular to the roll axis relocates the whole bundle instead of paying wound fabric out, and the distal lobe travels with the gripper rather than staying seated. Treat such an outcome as two separate findings: the grounding, engagement depth, approach clearance, fixed wrist orientation and quasi-static release are validated because cloth was held and carried and must be reused unchanged, while the terminal end-cap joins the retired anchor classes alongside the high-relief core, the planar raised shelf, the flat perimeter lip and the steep fold wall. Do not re-tune pull direction or pull distance after such a result, since no layer was isolated and the carry tested nothing. Require either a mechanically verified free fabric boundary with visible interior passage between plies, or opposition supplied by immobilizing material well away from the separation point, before the next lift. Also treat a deposit that lands back over a feature the previous view had exposed as an unhelpful laydown, and place the next deposit farther out on clear surface.

### Skill: collar-full-shake (v1)
Purpose: Use a validated shirt-collar grasp to lift, shake open, transport, and lay the garment down so the collar structure can reveal the garment.
Guidance:
Use only after the visual collar decision and grounded Camera A grasp are validated. Keep the collar grasp orientation fixed and perpendicular to the collar. Lift to a controller-reachable high pose, center at Y=0, perform the host-owned shake-open maneuver, then move toward a useful +X location before retreating toward -X while descending through several waypoints. Keep descent and retreat balanced rather than making either one dominate, release only near the table after the garment has had room to spread, and retract/home afterward. Use current measured geometry and controller IK; never copy fixed coordinates, release in mid-air, or replace the collar with a shoulder or sleeve.

### Skill: controller-ik-recovery (v1)
Purpose: Recover safely when controller IK rejects a garment manipulation path before physical execution.
Guidance:
When controller IK rejects a pose or interpolated segment, preserve the supported visual objective but shorten extreme reach, lift, or transport; keep every waypoint inside the workspace, include a controlled release, and rerun preflight and controller IK before execution.

### Skill: direct-shake (v1)

Guidance:

### Skill: flatten-garment (v1)
Purpose: Progressively open and flatten a garment by validating the grasped structure, establishing a useful hanging configuration, transporting in a verified opening direction, and laying down only while the scene shows measurable improvement.
Guidance:
Follow this staged workflow:
1. Acquire a validated garment structure: choose a visible, liftable anchor whose local RGB-D measurement, height, and depth consistency support a real garment grasp; do not proceed from an unsupported or table-only point.
2. Establish a hanging configuration if useful: lift to a validated safe height and confirm that the grasped fabric is supported and can hang without dragging or colliding. If the lift does not reveal a supported structure, stop and re-plan.
3. Transport toward a verified opening direction: infer the direction from the current garment geometry and before/after evidence, then use validated intermediate waypoints with stable orientation and workspace margin. The farthest safe X direction is allowed only when the scene verifies that it opens the garment; do not assume it is always correct.
4. Continue only while overlap decreases or coverage increases: after each meaningful transport segment, compare the garment footprint, visible area, layer overlap, and height relief. Stop, release, or re-plan when the move is not improving those measures; never continue a blind pull.
5. Lay down progressively: retreat while descending through validated intermediate heights, release quasi-statically on a clean surface, and avoid dropping, flinging, twisting, or dragging the loaded gripper. The skill supplies this decision sequence, never fixed coordinates or robot API calls.

### Skill: grounding-plan-recovery (v1)
Purpose: Recover from an invalid or inconsistent grounded garment proposal before motion.
Guidance:
When grounding validation rejects a selected point or its use in the plan, reinspect the current evidence, choose a newly grounded visible fabric point, keep the path inside the workspace, include a controlled release, and rerun preflight and IK before execution.

### Skill: hold-checkpoint-timeout-recovery (v1)

Guidance:
Keep the existing rules: a failed-closed or timed-out hold check makes the observation evidence about the grasp only, the unexecuted transport must never be recorded as wrong in direction or distance, and the validated approach clearance, deposit region and quasi-static release carry over to the retry. Add this definitive escalation threshold with infrastructure acknowledgment: when a configuration has produced 15 or more consecutive acquisition failures across at least 5 geometrically distinct anchor classes (peaks, boundary bands, low-relief structures, raised rims, corners, raised edges, claimed free boundary lips) where adequate engagement depth was achieved (closure commanded at or below measured surface height, including compression-probe-recommended depths for high-relief structures and manual calculation for low-relief structures) and every attempt confirms no independent hanging material with all far landmarks remaining seated and hold checkpoint returning FAILED_CLOSED or timeout, treat this as definitive evidence that the garment configuration does not provide separable single-anchor structure. ### Skill: laydown (v2)
Purpose: Convert a garment held from a useful lifting anchor into a more spread tabletop configuration, and recognise when a release has re-piled the garment onto itself instead of opening it.
Guidance:
Keep the quasi-static procedure: let the garment hang under gravity, retreat away from the hanging cloth while descending through intermediate heights, let the hanging face become the upward face, and release in a controlled way. Add two checks. First, before descending, require the retreat to carry the grasp point beyond the horizontal extent of the material still hanging below it, onto clear table, so the fabric unrolls onto bare surface rather than settling back over the area it came from; a retreat shorter than the hanging garment's own reach should be treated as not ready for release. Second, after release, compare footprints rather than only position: if the deposited outline sits inside the previous outline, if previously exposed features such as prints, collars or hems have become covered, and if new steep fold walls appear in depth, judge the laydown a regression caused by too short a retreat, and plan the next deposit farther out across clean table instead of repeating the same descent from the same anchor.

skill_update.name: null-change-missed-grasp-recovery
skill_update.purpose: Recognise a near-null garment action, separate a clean miss from a contact-without-hold on a compressible pile, reject a closure whose resolved anchor or engaged height is inconsistent with the visually chosen structure, and additionally reject local loft on a flat single-layer panel as grounds for an interior pinch.
skill_update.guidance: Keep all existing null-change, contact-without-hold, escalation, and pre-closure consistency checks. Add a flat-panel loft caveat. When a garment lies fully spread as a single layer and the only pre-action support for a chosen contact is a modest local height rise above the table, treat that rise as a lofted wrinkle in continuous cloth rather than evidence of a separable ply, and do not plan a symmetric interior pinch there. Height inside the measured relief of such a patch can be correct while the closure still comes up empty, because the jaws have no fabric boundary to gather. If a null change follows that kind of interior contact, do not diagnose it as a depth problem or repeat it lower; record it as evidence about the contact hypothesis only, leave the untested pull direction, pull distance, deposit region and release choices intact, and re-ground the next attempt on a boundary the images actually show, such as a cuff or hem edge with bare surface visible beyond it, closing across that boundary rather than across open panel.
skill_update.rationale: This run closed at a depth already inside the measured cloth thickness at the chosen anchor and still produced a completely null result, which shows the existing height-consistency gate is necessary but not sufficient. Encoding the flat-panel loft caveat prevents the common wrong inference of another height-only retry and redirects the next attempt to a verified fabric boundary, which is reusable across any spread-garment first fold rather than specific to this experiment.

Begin above bare table outboard of the visible cuff boundary, clear of all fabric, and descend there to a low standoff just above table height so nothing sweeps across the sleeve on the way in. proposal.garment_observation: Camera A upright shows the dark navy short-sleeve tee still fully spread and frontal on the white table: collar near top centre, the square pixel-art chest print filling the torso mid-panel, and two short sleeve lobes projecting left and right. Every landmark matches the three saved iterations, so the garment is provably undisturbed and no fold step is complete. The selected anchor R110 sits at Camera-A pixel (455, 695) on the outer image-left sleeve, mid-height in the leftmost on-garment column, just inboard of the sleeve's free distal boundary with bare table beyond. Its measurement is informative: base XY (472.26, -256.53) mm, table at 2.55 mm, fabric top at 22.15 mm, i.e. 19.60 mm of relief. That is roughly twice to five times the relief measured at the three previously failed contacts (9.59 mm interior loft, 4.17 mm cuff column, 8.11 mm gathered region), so this stretch of the cuff/hem region stands genuinely proud of the table as a lofted lip rather than lying as a flat sheet. A lip that tall implies real interior passage underneath it, which is the mechanically verifiable structure the last evaluation asked for.
proposal.reveal_strategy: This serves fold step 1, left sleeve inward, and nothing else. Three clean empty closes have exhausted the top-down single-contact families on this lobe (yaw 0 interior pinch, yaw 90 edge-straddle, yaw 45 gather-then-pinch), and every one closed at a height already inside the measured relief, so grasp Z is not the experiment. Three variables change together here. Contact XY moves out to the R110 lofted cuff region, about 46 mm from the iteration-3 contact and on 19.60 mm of relief instead of 4-9 mm. Jaw azimuth goes to the untested 135 deg so the closing axis crosses the local hem tangent diagonally rather than lying along an edge it already failed on. And the pre-close entry path becomes genuinely sub-plane: the tool descends to z = 4.5 mm while still outboard over bare table at y = -278, then sweeps inboard 25.5 mm at that low height so the leading jaw tip passes beneath the 22.15 mm fabric top and into the space under the lip, with closure commanded at the end of that sweep while the lip is still standing on the tip. The final pre-close centre (472.3, -252.5) sits 4.0 mm inboard of the R110 anchor, within the allowed 10 mm learned offset, and deliberately inside the cloth rather than straddling over table, per the iteration-2 lesson. Because acquisition has never validated, this stays the smallest reversible probe: a controller-valid observable first lift of 28.0 mm (from z = 4.5 to 32.5), which is inside the required 15-30 mm probe band and still well above the 10-11 mm lifts of iterations 2 and 3, then only 8.5 mm of inboard tension to test whether the sleeve follows, then lower and release in place. The inward transport toward the torso centreline (+base_y, roughly 110-140 mm along the cuff-to-armhole axis) remains untested and is deliberately held back for the expansion iteration.

decision.garment_observation: Camera A upright shows a dark navy short-sleeve tee lying flat and roughly frontal on a white table: collar/neck tape near the top centre, a square multi-panel pixel-art chest print filling the torso mid-panel, and two short sleeve lobes projecting left and right from the shoulders. The image-left sleeve lobe runs from its armhole (around the R084/R071 column) outboard to a free distal boundary at the far image-left, where the leftmost cyan column (R108, R109, R110, R111) sits on sleeve cloth with clear bare white table immediately beyond. Along that distal boundary the RGB shows a narrow brighter rim and a slight tonal step relative to the open sleeve panel, consistent with a hemmed cuff band (two plies) standing marginally proud of the table rather than a single feathered sheet edge. Inboard of it, the sleeve panel is smooth and low-relief with only faint shoulder-line wrinkling. Comparing against the three saved iterations, every landmark (collar, print, sleeve label, both lobes, silhouette) is in the same place: the garment is provably undisturbed, which matches three clean empty closes and means no fold progress exists yet. The magenta MOLMO point sits on the upper-outer image-left sleeve, so it agrees with the sleeve region topologically, but it lands very near where iterations 1 and 3 already closed empty, so I use it only to confirm the lobe identity, not to choose contact.
decision.opening_strategy: Stay on the five-step ledger: this iteration serves step 1, left sleeve inward, and nothing else. Three failures have already eliminated the plausible single-contact top-down families on this lobe: a symmetric interior pinch on the mid-panel loft (yaw 0, vertical), an outboard edge-straddle at the cuff column (yaw 90, 8 mm lateral), and a gather-then-pinch after a low inboard sweep (yaw 45). All three closed at heights already inside the measured cloth relief, so grasp Z is not the open variable and must not be the experiment. The materially new hypothesis is mechanical, not positional-only: bite the sleeve's own hem band from underneath. Instead of pressing a jaw pair down onto cloth that flattens away, the leading jaw tip should arrive from outside the distal sleeve boundary, travelling low and slightly upward-inboard so its tip passes beneath the hem's raised lip and into the interior passage between the two plies, with the TCP centre sitting clearly on cloth (a few mm inboard of the boundary) rather than straddling it over table. Closure happens during that short inboard sweep while the hem lip is still standing on the tip, not after settling into a static pose. Jaw azimuth moves to an untested oblique value (~135 deg / -45 deg) so the closing axis crosses the local hem tangent diagonally and one tip captures a diagonal bite of the band. Because acquisition has never validated, this stays a smallest-reversible probe: acquire, lift clear enough to read unambiguously, then lower and release if empty. The inward transport itself remains untested and is deliberately left unchanged for the expansion iteration.

It is not on the torso interior, chest print, collar, neck label, or the opposite sleeve. I chose it over the inboard column (R096-R100), which sits on the open sleeve panel and the underarm notch region already contacted empty in iterations 1 and 3 and where MOLMO also points, and over R108 (nearer the shoulder/sleeve top corner, where the boundary curves into the shoulder line and the panel is more strongly supported) and R111 (the lower outer corner, closest in the outboard-inferior direction to the failed iteration-2 straddle contact, and a corner bite risks capturing only a small tab). R110 gives the cleanest straight run of hem band with unobstructed table on the approach side, so a low sub-plane entry can travel over bare table and slip under the lip without the tool ever passing over the print or collar, and mid-cuff is also the natural lever point for swinging the sleeve inward along the cuff-to-armhole axis in the follow-on fold.

decision.motion_intent: Approach from outboard of the image-left sleeve boundary, entirely over bare table, with the wrist held at the untested oblique azimuth (about 135 deg / -45 deg) so the jaw closing axis crosses the local hem tangent diagonally. Descend outside the cloth first, then convert to a shallow, near-horizontal final segment that travels inboard toward the garment (+base_y sense, toward the torso centreline) so the leading jaw tip slides beneath the raised hem lip rather than pressing down on flat cloth; the pre-close entry path, not the height, is the changed variable. Command closure during that short inboard sweep of roughly 10-15 mm, with the TCP centre ending a few mm inside the cloth boundary so the hem is gathered between the jaws instead of split by the jaw gap. Hold yaw constant from before closure through the whole probe so the wrist never winds the fabric. Then perform a lift-only reversible probe: rise straight up 35-45 mm, clearly higher than the 10-24 mm lifts used before, so a held cuff must show as a tent, hanging patch, or shadow gap in the checkpoint frames; add at most a few millimetres of inboard tension at the top to test whether the sleeve actually follows. If the checkpoint shows fabric held, the retained plan for the next iteration is inward transport along the cuff-to-armhole axis toward the torso centreline for roughly 110-140 mm, constant yaw, then controlled descent and release over the torso so the sleeve lies flat across the chest panel. If nothing is held, lower along the same path and open in place so the garment stays exactly as observed. Host remains authoritative for calibration, workspace limits, grasp height, preflight, and IK.
decision.expected_observation: If the sub-plane hem bite works, the lift checkpoint frames should show the image-left cuff band no longer flat: a raised tent or hanging flap of dark cloth directly under the jaws, a visible shadow gap between that cloth and the table, and the sleeve boundary pulled a short distance inboard from its previously seated outline while the collar, chest print, sleeve label, and right sleeve stay put. Height/relief evidence should show a localized elevated cloth mass beside or beneath the tool rather than only the arm intruding on an unchanged background gradient. If the probe fails again, the contact sheet will look like the three prior runs: every landmark seated, no tent, no hanging patch, tool clear of the table while the hem stays flat, which would then rule out sub-plane single-contact hem entry as well and push the next hypothesis toward true opposition (pin the sleeve with one contact while a second separates) or a different named boundary such as the bottom hem band.
safety_notes: Keep the whole approach and retreat corridor over bare white table outboard of the image-left sleeve; the tool must never pass over the chest print, collar, or neck label.
This is a reversible probe: if the lift checkpoint shows nothing held, lower along the same path and open the jaws in place so the garment stays in its currently observed pose.
Do not use grasp Z as the experiment variable; three closes already happened inside the measured cloth relief, so the change must be contact XY, jaw azimuth, and the pre-close entry path.
Limit the low inboard sweep to roughly 10-15 mm so a failed attempt cannot drag or displace the whole garment or disturb the still-unfolded torso and right sleeve.
Keep down-force low on the final shallow segment; the jaw tip should skim the table to get under the hem lip, not scrape or wedge into it.
Hold yaw constant from before closure through lift and any descent so the wrist does not wind or twist the sleeve.
Abort and release in place if the garment silhouette shifts wholesale or the sleeve starts sliding rather than lifting, then request a fresh observation before retrying.
Stay well inside workspace and IK limits on the outboard approach; the host retains authority for calibration, grasp height, preflight, and execution.
No pulling or stretching of the sleeve while grip validity is unknown; a single ply of thin jersey can tear or roll if tensioned by a partial bite.

In frames #10-#12 dark material appears immediately adjacent to the gripper column, but it cannot be separated from the sleeve merely lying against the tool versus being carried by it.
The depth halves in #11-#13 are dominated by large black invalid regions coincident with the arm, so they neither confirm nor exclude an elevated cloth mass beside the tool.
Net: fabric moved, but sustained support through the 28 mm lift is not visually demonstrated, which is the specific claim under test.
The intended structure was a local bite of the lofted image-left cuff/hem lip with interior passage underneath, which would appear as an isolated raised patch while far landmarks stayed seated.
Instead the after RGB shows the garment as a whole slightly repositioned: collar, chest print, and both sleeve lobes shift together, which is a drag signature rather than ply isolation.
No residual isolated cuff deformation, standing lip, or separated ply is visible at the contact region in the after view; the sleeve boundary is still a single continuous flat edge.
Camera B after confirms the shirt remains one flat single-layer panel with the print fully exposed and the sleeve lying flat, so no local structure was separated and retained.
Transport was intentionally not executed in the reversible acquisition probe.
The probe reversed and released at the original contact instead of laying down a fold.

keep: The five-step fold objective and left_sleeve as the earliest incomplete step; no reordering.
Camera A as the grounding view and the outer image-left sleeve/cuff region as the named target.
The R110 lofted-relief contact region, which for the first time in four attempts produced a visible fabric response.
The sub-plane low entry over bare table that arrives from outboard and keeps the tool clear of the chest print and collar.
The inward +base_y transport direction toward the torso centreline, still untested and uncontradicted.
Constant yaw through the probe and the reversible lift-then-lower-then-release discipline.
change: Opposition: the drag signature shows the sheet slid as a whole instead of a ply separating, so add a second contact that pins or tensions the sleeve inboard of the bite while the acquiring jaw closes.
Closure geometry: the 4 mm inboard centre on a 19.60 mm lip still did not isolate a ply; bias the closure so one jaw is demonstrably beneath the lip and the other above it.
Jaw alignment: 0, 45, 90 and now 135 deg are all tried, so azimuth-only variation is uninformative and should change only together with the opposition change.

Anti-slip conditioning: shorten the inboard sweep and add a brief static settle against the lip before closing, since a 25.5 mm low sweep appears to have pushed the garment rather than tunnelled under it.
Alternative boundary: if single-contact is retained, move to the bottom hem band where two plies and the gap between them are directly visible rather than inferred from relief alone.
next_experiment.reason: This attempt is causally different from the three preceding ones: it is the first that left a persistent garment change, so contact XY on the high-relief cuff region and the sub-plane entry did reach fabric. But the change is whole-garment displacement, not a lifted or isolated ply, which localises the remaining fault to closure geometry and the absence of opposition rather than to contact location, azimuth, or Z. Height remains inadmissible as the next variable: the closure at 4.5 mm sat far inside a 19.60 mm relief lip above a 2.55 mm table and still failed to isolate cloth. Azimuth is also exhausted as a standalone variable with four values tested. The unexplained mechanism is that a single jaw pair closing on an unanchored sheet lets the whole garment slide, so the next experiment must supply opposition or a verifiable two-ply gap, and should shorten the sweep so the tool settles against the lip instead of pushing the garment ahead of it.

evidence: Acquisition-only evaluation did not reassess semantic target selection.

Before/after Camera-A RGB are not identical this time: the image-left sleeve lobe and the lower-left silhouette sit in visibly different positions and the chest print has shifted slightly toward image-right, so the tool did engage fabric rather than closing on pure empty space.

No lift-checkpoint frame (#09-#13, tool highest over the contact) shows the unambiguous supported-cloth signature: no clear tent, no hanging flap below the jaws, no distinct shadow gap between raised cloth and the table.
In frames #10-#12 dark material appears immediately adjacent to the gripper column, but it cannot be separated from the sleeve merely lying against the tool versus being carried by it.
The depth halves in #11-#13 are dominated by large black invalid regions coincident with the arm, so they neither confirm nor exclude an elevated cloth mass beside the tool.
Net: fabric moved, but sustained support through the 28 mm lift is not visually demonstrated, which is the specific claim under test.
The intended structure was a local bite of the lofted image-left cuff/hem lip with interior passage underneath, which would appear as an isolated raised patch while far landmarks stayed seated.
Instead the after RGB shows the garment as a whole slightly repositioned: collar, chest print, and both sleeve lobes shift together, which is a drag signature rather than ply isolation.
No residual isolated cuff deformation, standing lip, or separated ply is visible at the contact region in the after view; the sleeve boundary is still a single continuous flat edge.
Camera B after confirms the shirt remains one flat single-layer panel with the print fully exposed and the sleeve lying flat, so no local structure was separated and retained.
Transport was intentionally not executed in the reversible acquisition probe.
The probe reversed and released at the original contact instead of laying down a fold.

Camera A as the grounding view and the outer image-left sleeve/cuff region as the named target.
The R110 lofted-relief contact region, which for the first time in four attempts produced a visible fabric response.
The sub-plane low entry over bare table that arrives from outboard and keeps the tool clear of the chest print and collar.

change: Opposition: the drag signature shows the sheet slid as a whole instead of a ply separating, so add a second contact that pins or tensions the sleeve inboard of the bite while the acquiring jaw closes.
Closure geometry: the 4 mm inboard centre on a 19.60 mm lip still did not isolate a ply; bias the closure so one jaw is demonstrably beneath the lip and the other above it.
Jaw alignment: 0, 45, 90 and now 135 deg are all tried, so azimuth-only variation is uninformative and should change only together with the opposition change.

Anti-slip conditioning: shorten the inboard sweep and add a brief static settle against the lip before closing, since a 25.5 mm low sweep appears to have pushed the garment rather than tunnelled under it.
Alternative boundary: if single-contact is retained, move to the bottom hem band where two plies and the gap between them are directly visible rather than inferred from relief alone.
next_experiment.reason: This attempt is causally different from the three preceding ones: it is the first that left a persistent garment change, so contact XY on the high-relief cuff region and the sub-plane entry did reach fabric. But the change is whole-garment displacement, not a lifted or isolated ply, which localises the remaining fault to closure geometry and the absence of opposition rather than to contact location, azimuth, or Z. Height remains inadmissible as the next variable: the closure at 4.5 mm sat far inside a 19.60 mm relief lip above a 2.55 mm table and still failed to isolate cloth. Azimuth is also exhausted as a standalone variable with four values tested. The unexplained mechanism is that a single jaw pair closing on an unanchored sheet lets the whole garment slide, so the next experiment must supply opposition or a verifiable two-ply gap, and should shorten the sweep so the tool settles against the lip instead of pushing the garment ahead of it.

Three clean empty closes have exhausted the top-down single-contact families on this lobe (yaw 0 interior pinch, yaw 90 edge-straddle, yaw 45 gather-then-pinch), and every one closed at a height already inside the measured relief, so grasp Z is not the experiment. Three variables change together here. Contact XY moves out to the R110 lofted cuff region, about 46 mm from the iteration-3 contact and on 19.60 mm of relief instead of 4-9 mm. Jaw azimuth goes to the untested 135 deg so the closing axis crosses the local hem tangent diagonally rather than lying along an edge it already failed on. And the pre-close entry path becomes genuinely sub-plane: the tool descends to z = 4.5 mm while still outboard over bare table at y = -278, then sweeps inboard 25.5 mm at that low height so the leading jaw tip passes beneath the 22.15 mm fabric top and into the space under the lip, with closure commanded at the end of that sweep while the lip is still standing on the tip. The final pre-close centre (472.3, -252.5) sits 4.0 mm inboard of the R110 anchor, within the allowed 10 mm learned offset, and deliberately inside the cloth rather than straddling over table, per the iteration-2 lesson. Because acquisition has never validated, this stays the smallest reversible probe: a controller-valid observable first lift of 28.0 mm (from z = 4.5 to 32.5), which is inside the required 15-30 mm probe band and still well above the 10-11 mm lifts of iterations 2 and 3, then only 8.5 mm of inboard tension to test whether the sleeve follows, then lower and release in place. The inward transport toward the torso centreline (+base_y, roughly 110-140 mm along the cuff-to-armhole axis) remains untested and is deliberately held back for the expansion iteration.

proposal.reveal_strategy: This serves fold step 1, left sleeve inward, only. Evidence to date: three clean empty closes (yaw 0 interior pinch, yaw 90 edge-straddle, yaw 45 gather-then-pinch), then a fourth that finally moved fabric but dragged the whole garment instead of isolating a ply. That localizes the fault to closure geometry and absent opposition, not height, and not azimuth alone (0/45/90/135 all spent). Grasp Z is inadmissible as the experiment: the last close sat at 4.5 mm inside a 19.6 mm lip and still failed. The new mechanism converts table friction into opposition. The tool first pins sleeve cloth at (430.5, -244.0), about 6.3 mm inboard of the R108 anchor, at z = 9.0 mm — light contact above the 5.19 mm table, enough to hold the sheet without denting it. It then makes a short 8 mm buckling push outboard to (430.5, -252.0) so fabric trapped between the pin and the free lip must stand rather than slide, far shorter than the 25.5 mm sweep that dragged the garment. It rises to z = 12.0 mm at that same XY so the jaw gap spans the standing lip with one jaw below and one above it, then closes. The final pre-close centre is 1.7 mm from the R108 anchor XY, well inside the 10 mm allowance. Yaw is 20 deg, an untested azimuth oblique to the local boundary tangent, held constant throughout. Probe discipline is preserved: lift 26.0 mm (z 12.0 to 38.0, inside the 15-30 mm observable band), only 6 mm of inboard tension to test whether the sleeve follows, then lower and open in place. Net lateral motion is 14 mm, inside the exploration budget. The inward transport toward the torso centreline (roughly 110-140 mm along the cuff-to-armhole axis) stays reserved for the expansion iteration once a hold is confirmed.

decision.opening_strategy: This iteration serves fold step 1, left sleeve inward, and nothing else. The tool first sets down lightly on cloth just inboard of the boundary to pin the sleeve against the table, then makes a very short buckling push of roughly 8 mm toward the lifted lip so pinned fabric has nowhere to slide and must stand into a fold, dwells briefly so the buckle settles rather than being chased, and only then closes with the jaw gap spanning the standing lip. decision.motion_intent: Approach from outboard of the image-left sleeve entirely over bare table, wrist at an azimuth not yet tried (roughly 20 deg, oblique to the local outer-boundary tangent rather than the spent 0/45/90/135), held constant from before closure through the whole probe so the wrist never winds cloth. Descend outside the cloth, then set a light pin contact on sleeve fabric a few millimetres inboard of the visible boundary, pressing just enough to hold the sheet against the table without denting it. From that pinned state make a very short buckling push of about 8 mm toward the lofted lip, far shorter than the 25.5 mm sweep that dragged the garment, so fabric between pin and free edge must stand rather than slide. Dwell briefly so the buckle settles, then close with the jaw gap spanning the standing lip, one jaw beneath it and one above it, which is the closure-geometry change the last evaluation called for. Lift straight up by an amount inside the controller's admissible 15-30 mm observable band, high enough that held cloth must read as a tent or hanging flap against the white table. At the top add only 5-8 mm of inboard tension toward the torso centreline to test whether the sleeve follows rather than the jaws sliding on it. Then reverse: lower along the same path to just above the contact and open in place. If a hold is confirmed, the retained expansion is inward transport along the cuff-to-armhole axis toward the torso centreline for roughly 110-140 mm at constant yaw, then controlled descent and release so the sleeve lies flat across the chest panel. decision.expected_observation: A successful pin-buckle-settle bite should show, at the lift checkpoints, dark cloth clearly raised off the table directly under the jaws: a tent or hanging flap with a shadow gap beneath it, and the outer image-left sleeve boundary drawn a few millimetres inboard during the small tension move, while the collar, chest print, sleeve label, right sleeve, and bottom hem all stay seated. Height/relief evidence should show a localized elevated cloth mass beside or beneath the tool rather than only the arm intruding on the background gradient. Two informative negatives must be distinguished. If every landmark again stays seated with no tent, single-contact acquisition on this sleeve is falsified even on a pre-buckled lofted edge, and the next hypothesis should move to the bottom hem band where two plies and their gap are directly visible. If instead the whole silhouette shifts again with no tent, the pin was insufficient and table friction alone cannot supply opposition, arguing for a dedicated pinning contact before any further bite here. Either way the probe reverses and releases at the contact, so the garment stays recoverable.
safety_notes: Keep the entire approach and retreat corridor over bare table outboard of the image-left sleeve; the tool must never pass over the chest print, collar, or neck label.
The garment was already displaced once by an over-long low sweep, so cap the buckling push at roughly 8 mm and abort if far landmarks (collar, print, right sleeve, hem) begin to move together again.

Grasp Z must not be the experiment variable: the previous close at 4.5 mm inside a 19.6 mm relief lip above a 2.55 mm table still failed, so the changes are contact XY, closure geometry, the pin-and-buckle mechanism, and jaw azimuth.
Reversible probe only: lower along the same path and open the jaws in place if the lift checkpoint shows nothing held, leaving the garment in its currently observed pose.
Keep the pin contact force light; it should hold the sheet against the table, not press a dent into the sleeve or scuff the fabric.
Hold yaw constant from before closure through lift, tension, and descent so the wrist never winds or twists the sleeve.
Keep the loaded inboard tension to a few millimetres while grip validity is unknown; a partial bite on thin jersey can roll or tear if pulled.
Never treat the magenta MOLMO point as a grasp target; it is only a fallible semantic hint used to focus attention on the lofted outer sleeve region.
Stay well inside workspace and IK limits on the outboard approach; the host retains authority for calibration, safe Z, preflight, and execution.

evidence: Acquisition-only evaluation did not reassess semantic target selection.

Before and after Camera-A RGB are indistinguishable: the tilted shoulder line, collar position, chest print placement, sleeve label, and both sleeve lobes occupy identical pixels, so nothing was carried or displaced.
In the lift-checkpoint frames (#09-#13, gripper highest over the contact) no cloth is raised beneath or beside the jaws: no tent, no hanging flap, no shadow gap between fabric and table.
The gripper is visibly clear of the table at those checkpoints while the outer image-left sleeve stays flat and seated, so the jaws rose empty rather than carrying the 21.4 mm-relief lip.
The depth halves in #10-#13 show only the arm as a large black/invalid intrusion against an unchanged background gradient; no elevated cloth mass appears adjacent to or under the tool.
Unlike the previous attempt there is not even a drag signature, so the pin-and-buckle push left no lasting contact effect at all.
The intended structure was a standing lofted lip of outer image-left sleeve fabric, pre-buckled by the pin-and-push, with the jaw gap spanning it.
No lift-checkpoint frame shows an isolated raised or hanging patch, so the separable-layer signature is absent while far landmarks stay seated.
The far landmarks (collar, chest print, right sleeve, bottom hem) also stay seated in every frame, so this is neither ply isolation nor whole-garment drag.

The after RGB shows the outer sleeve boundary as a single continuous flat edge with no residual buckle, standing ridge, or crease where the 8 mm push passed, so the intended pre-buckled structure was not even created, let alone acquired.
Transport was intentionally not executed in the reversible acquisition probe.

Notably this attempt produced even less effect than the previous one, which at least dragged the garment, indicating that measured relief on this sleeve does not correspond to real graspable air and that pinning against table friction supplies no usable opposition. The unexplained mechanism is the absence of a verifiable two-ply opening, so the next experiment should relocate to the bottom hem band where plies and their gap are visible in RGB, or introduce genuine dual-contact opposition, rather than retuning any parameter of the current single-contact scheme.
